Researchers have observed unusual diffusion patterns during experiments with the flowing of fluids through complex, irregular porous materials that deviate from typical Gaussian behavior. This paper aims to theoretically investigate the mechanisms responsible for these abnormal diffusion patterns, specifically focusing on random porous media in one-dimensional settings. A model was created to simulate a scenario in which a fluid undergoes diffusion based on the local properties of the materials, with random permeability properties modeled in two ways: as discrete jumps following an exponential distribution or as smooth fractional Brownian motion. The mathematical analysis of both models revealed characteristic non-standard scaling laws in accordance with the observed experimental results.

Building a high-quality superconducting qubit resonator demands an in-depth understanding of how electromagnetic field patterns interact with the qubit's dipole and the process of Kerr nonlinear photon coupling. This paper presents a general approach for both linear and Kerr nonlinear coupling in resonator-qudit systems, utilizing paraxial equations from optical science. Our method involves applying a quality function to measure the degree of coupling and utilizing first and second variational principles to find optimal field patterns that maximize coupling. These principles allow for the derivation of key equations that characterize the field patterns, ultimately revealing their unique properties. As a result, our approach not only provides insight into the fundamental behavior of electromagnetic field patterns but also facilitates comparison and study across different types of resonator-qudit systems.

Lyapunov methods are a well-established framework for assessing the stability of nonlinear control systems. However, these methods have a critical shortcoming in that they can only provide insights into system behavior over time, not finite convergence. This limitation makes it challenging to design control systems that reach their desired state within a predetermined timeframe. To overcome this issue, the linear Lyapunov function combined with unbounded controls has proven ineffective. This issue is rectified in this paper, which introduces convex Lyapunov functions to achieve finite convergence and facilitates the development of control systems that can achieve their target within a predetermined timeframe. Building on this approach, we develop a convex program to synthesize unbounded controls, leveraging these functions to facilitate design and analysis. These tools enable us to prove that the systems will converge to their intended state, even in the face of unbounded controls. Finally, we demonstrate the practical application of our methods through a case study on multi-agent flocking systems.

This research utilizes a generative adversarial network to recover fine details in velocity measurements of fluid flow in confined spaces under different flow conditions. We trained the model on three flow cases at Reynolds numbers of 10,000, 20,000, and 40,000, evaluating it against high-resolution measurements. The results show that the network accurately reproduces small-scale velocity patterns, with a mean error rate under 0.02 for a Reynolds number up to 40,000. We also tested the model's ability to generalize to new Reynolds numbers, successfully predicting flow at a Reynolds number of 60,000 with a mean error rate of 0.04. A physics-informed training loss successfully reduced the error rate by half compared to a standard $l_1$-norm loss.

This article focuses on the study of time-dependent wave equations, particularly those described by second-order time derivatives, in the context of relativistic and non-relativistic theories. In classical physics, a well-posed problem can be found for both the time-dependent scalar wave equation and the time-dependent Schrödinger equation. In contrast, many time-dependent non-relativistic theories, such as elastic mechanics, cannot be directly converted into a corresponding relativistic theory without encountering mathematical inconsistencies. Some of the issues with this conversion are discussed in this article. In addition, conditions under which the combined conservation of energy and momentum can be satisfied in elastic mechanics are examined. Finally, the existence of coherent elastic waves that maintain their shape and travel at finite speeds is analyzed in the context of special relativity.

The success of machine learning systems is frequently hindered by training data limitations, particularly in accounting for new classes. Traditional approaches relying on explicit modeling of class-aggregate information are often impractical due to their low efficiency. To overcome this, an implicit approach is proposed that uses energy functions to model data distribution beyond training data, allowing the system to implicitly recognize novel classes with lower energy values. This paper presents a novel, implicit strategy for handling multi-class data with high uncertainty. By focusing on the energy function of the system, we aim to provide a reliable method for identifying and managing data that has high uncertainty and belongs to novel classes. A key innovation proposed is a multi-class uncertainty metric that is sensitive to energy levels and is informed by training data class frequencies. This is in contrast to previous approaches that only consider novel classes with lower energy values. To validate the proposed approach, we present an assurance calibration framework for assurance calibration using the proposed metric in conjunction with a probabilistic check. By calibrating the check to adjust its readings to match the proposed metric, we can adjust the check's reliability to reflect systems that have not been encountered before.

To train reinforcement learning agents on high-frequency sensor data for
long periods, we need to create virtual testing scenarios that closely mimic
real-world conditions. Our new platform, L2Explorer, is an advanced evaluation
system for reinforcement learning based on a fully digital testing scenario.
Built using the Simala simulation framework, it offers a high-quality virtual
environment where the learning algorithm can be continuously refined and
applied to new, unseen testing scenarios. As a result, we provide the best possible
conditions for developing reinforcement learning agents using continuous
frequency sensor data.

One of the key challenges in modeling complex systems lies in managing their high levels of variability and unpredictability. Processes based on natural language can effectively address this challenge by providing a declarative and natural language description of complex processes. However, they are limited in dealing with non-deterministic and irrational choices due to their inherent inflexibility. This issue is compounded when processes need to be optimized for specific goals, as their unoptimized nature often hinders their efficiency and effectiveness. This paper proposes a novel approach that combines processes based on natural language with probabilistic Markov decision processes to create an enhanced process model capable of meeting these demands. This approach not only provides a flexible and optimized process model but also ensures its soundness relative to the process based on natural language, thus preserving its declarative and natural language-like properties. To illustrate the practical applicability of this approach, the paper includes a case study on the reimbursement process, demonstrating its ability to balance efficiency, compliance, and customer-centricity.

In one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals, light propagation characteristics change dramatically at certain points, indicating a transition from quasi-bound to broken modes. This phenomenon occurs because the quasiperiodic structure causes a reclassification of modes from localized to extended. Our research indicates that adding transverse heterogeneity to this structure can cause photonic modes to transition from quasi-bound to quasi-bound again, effectively increasing their space. This is achieved by creating an overlap between previously disjoint modes, which can be utilized to manipulate and control photonic quasi-bound states for practical applications in photonic quasicrystals.

Liger, a high-performance adaptive optics system at the Keck Observatory, utilizes an infrared detector array to enhance its adaptive optics performance. However, handling and processing the vast amount of data it produces requires a robust method. A key feature of Liger is its ability to simultaneously record the infrared data and the visible light from the adaptive optics system, which uses a single-mode fiber. To effectively use this capability, real-time image processing is essential. This paper outlines our approach to using the Rosetta software to manage data processing, real-time image processing, and the connection with the Liger software, which is built upon the Qt framework.

Our research showcases the potential of using entangled photon pairs in a new type of spatial mode demultiplexing technique, allowing for precise measurement of small shifts in a diffraction grating beyond its usual limit. By analyzing the two photons' interference patterns, we achieve an remarkable improvement, sensing minute displacements equivalent to just a few nanometers.
This note provides an overview of various approaches to compactifying algebraic and geometric moduli spaces, with a focus on metric geometry.

An ecosystem's stability is intricately linked to the fluctuations experienced by its species. This relationship is well-documented for sudden, short-term transitions but less understood regarding gradual, long-term fluctuations and their impact on system predictability. A significant challenge arises from the conflicting effects of noise generated by rapid and slow fluctuations on system dynamics. To navigate this complexity, a simplified model was created, incorporating a logistic growth model modified to account for distinct short-term and long-term dynamics. This model is then analyzed to determine its noise characteristics and predictive capacity for a switching regime. Notably, it is found that the model exhibits a critical slowdown preceding slow transitions, accompanied by an increase in variability, whereas an abrupt decrease in fluctuations is indicative of abrupt, sudden transitions. These findings are subsequently applied to a dataset of deer population data, collected over a 60-year period, to detect patterns that may signal impending major population changes.

New simulations using an extended model for stellar bulges in our cosmological simulation have revealed a significant relationship between specific far-ultraviolet continuum and stellar mass at various stellar masses. This model, which incorporates a critical threshold for star formation within spheroidal galaxies, aligns well with observations from the CANDELS survey, particularly in the stellar mass range from 10^9 to 10^{11} solar masses. A key factor in this analysis is a distinct correlation between stellar bulge mass and total stellar mass that emerges at different stellar masses. The study reveals that galaxies with disk masses exceeding 10^{11} solar masses, characterized by significant stellar bulges, exhibit elevated star formation rates and a higher frequency of ongoing star formation compared to gas-rich but star formation-inactive galaxies with smaller bulges. This discrepancy may be explained by star formation in the central regions of massive galaxies being suppressed due to gas stabilization in their dense stellar cores.

Our research focuses on developing effective techniques for cross-linguistic sentiment assessment, specifically examining the interplay between languages and its impact on sentiment classification. We examine multiple languages and tasks, exploring how data abundance and language difficulty influence the performance of neural networks in generating and classifying sentiment. Our findings are based on six languages and six tasks, with the data drawn from social media posts. To simplify the process, we utilize pre-trained word embeddings for each language, which are then combined into a single multilingual word vector space. Our primary objective is to determine the most effective strategies for simultaneous training across languages and tasks. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of various simultaneous training approaches, including the use of task-specific and language-specific embedding layers, as well as attention mechanisms for embedding selection. We also compare these approaches with trained models. As a result, we provide the sentiment classification performance of embedding models across languages and tasks, along with the outcome of multi-task training using a single language embedding layer.

Our research proposes a new technique for removing security barriers in Java applications, which we call Mending Barriers (MB). Specifically, MB can allow high-integrity code to bypass the limitations imposed by code with lower integrity in the presence of a security barrier removal, reminiscent of capabilities in other security models. Unlike the approach to eliminate security checks in Mendable Java, our technique doesn't assume the code with lower integrity is free of bugs or malicious software. Instead, a static analysis determines which security barriers can be safely removed, and the necessary checks are then automatically added to the code with higher integrity. In contrast to the approach to prevent capacity violations in Attache, our technique validates the security assumptions made in the code with higher integrity. Through a series of experiments, our results indicate that our methodology successfully eliminates security checks in 14 cases across 10 open-source Java applications and has a minimal impact on runtime performance, incurring an average increase of merely 1.05 milliseconds.

Given integers $a$ and $b$ within the range of natural numbers, we define a restricted sumset as $^{*}A+B=^{*}\{a+b\mid a\in A,\ b\in B,\ a\not=b\}$. In this study, we improve a well-known result by Freiman from 2004, which established that for sufficiently large natural numbers $k$, if the cardinality of a restricted sumset $^{*}A$ where $A$ is a subset of natural numbers satisfies the condition $^{*}A+A=^{*}\{a+b\mid a\in A,\ b\in A,\ a\not=b\}$, and meets the cardinality constraint $^{*}A+A\leqslant \frac{8}{3}(A-1)$, then $^{*}A$ can be represented as two consecutive sequences of integers $^{*}A=^{*}\{a,a+1,\cdots,a+b-1,a+b,\cdots,a+b+c-1\}$, with the cardinality relationship $\card{A}\leqslant \frac{3}{5}\card{C}$ being obtained.

Consider a stochastic process defined by the equation Y_t = (X_t - t)/sqrt(t), where (X_t) is a fractional Brownian motion with Hurst parameter H in the interval (0,1). Let the set sigma consist of all values y for which the probability of (Y_t = y for some time t in the interval [0,1]) is 1. Our research indicates that the integral of the probability density of Y_t over the set sigma is greater than zero, and there exists a point y0 in the interval [0,inf) for which the set of times when (Y_t = y0) is a closed interval of positive length.

This research explores the impact of quantum fluctuations in a system modeled after H\'enon-Heiles, particularly focusing on how the H\'enon parameter influences quantum fluctuations and hampers the effectiveness of certain approximation techniques. We apply Dirac's variational principle to obtain more accurate results, and examine the H\'enon-Heiles system's behavior using H\'enon parameter and classical enargy. Furthermore, we introduce a modified approach incorporating the Jackiw-Kerman function to analyze and predict the critical point of quantum focus-demotion in the H\'enon parameter.

X-ray images of COVID-19 patients can be used to predict whether they will need intensive care, as research into this area is still in its early stages. We are looking for the specific features in those images that show signs of severe illness and possible signs of organ failure. We are employing advanced techniques to find these key characteristics, which may include a combination of unsupervised and supervised learning methods. We will present our findings through visual representations and statistical analysis using scatter plots, scatter-matrix plots, and bar charts.
This research establishes that the simplicial group structure theorem applies to simplicial bundles globally, mirroring a key finding from the path-space simplicial group theorem.

Conventional Visual Relationship Detection (VRD) systems struggle with accuracy, resulting in numerous incorrect findings due to their limited scope in area and depth. Furthermore, the manual annotation of relationships requires a laborious process. To address these challenges, we introduce the Conquering Erroneous Positives in VRD (CEP-VRD) framework, an innovative detection-only strategy. Specifically, Converse Learning is designed to identify and classify potential relationships automatically, then we expand the conceptions of object-object interactions by categorizing Converse Pairs into distinct relationships according to their spatial location, physical, functional connections, and common sense, resulting in a significant increase in detected relationships without the need for time-consuming manual labeling. As a result, the detected Converse Pairs are classified as VRD relationships based on their spatial location, physical, functional connections, and common sense, leading to a notable increase in the number of relationships detected, yielding an 11.5% improvement in the PASCAL-VR dataset's mean average precision. Converse Learning is then guided by a dual learning mechanism that identifies and addresses potential relationships automatically, allowing the system to expand the conceptions of object-object interactions without the need for time-consuming manual labeling. As a result, the detected Converse Pairs are classified as VRD relationships according to their spatial location, physical, functional connections, and common sense, leading to a significant increase in the number of relationships detected, resulting in an 11.5%

This study enhances the efficiency of deep learning algorithms for activity recognition in low-light conditions with limited training data. By pre-training a state-of-the-art model on the UCF CR-5 dataset under high-light conditions, we demonstrate the effectiveness of reduced training and data sets under low-light environments. Specifically, modifying the number of negative samples and training images for fine-tuning optimizes the performance and speeds up the training process. Our experiments show that R-BERT, the optimized model, outperforms the original BERT-based algorithm while requiring significantly fewer computational resources.

Traditional FPGAs are highly versatile, offering developers the ability to create highly optimized and versatile processors. A novel dataflow computing model has been introduced, combining a concurrent programming approach, specifically dataflow, with an efficient memory architecture. This model allows processors to operate on large blocks of data stored in on-chip memory, eliminating the need for extensive interconnects and small instruction caches. By utilizing large data blocks, the processors can minimize the overhead associated with data management, allowing them to operate at a high clock frequency. This model has been implemented in a processor, achieving a high clock frequency of 200MHz and the ability to process large amounts of data efficiently. When compared to other platforms, the processors demonstrated superior performance in image processing tasks, outperforming a commercially available microcontroller and a high-end laptop.

At redshifts greater than two, many galaxies that are located within high-density environments show a preference for being both massive and disk-shaped, often presenting an unusual flat rotation curve while still in a state of lopsidedness. This work centers on NGC3276, a galaxy that is situated within the Coma cluster at a redshift of approximately 2.955. It is characterized by a massive, lopsided, and disk-shaped structure that resides below its host galaxy's main body, yet maintains evidence of ongoing star formation within itself. By utilizing NGC3276 as an example, this study aims to explore the process of galaxy assembly during the early stages of the universe's history. Comparisons of NGC3276 with other NGC4486-morphological components that exhibit similar characteristics show that they share several similarities, despite each being unique. Additionally, by using NGC3276 and other components to model the process of galaxy assembly while being located within a galaxy cluster, this ALeRCE catalog identified several candidates that share several characteristics, in terms of their physical properties and locations within the cluster, with NGC3276. By comparing NGC3276 to other similar galaxies that are located within the cluster, it is found that NGC3276 is less massive than the average, but presents several distinguishing features, in terms of its star formation rate, velocity dispersion, and

We employ both existing and newly acquired data to investigate the possibility of a connected component in parameter space that includes a signal region, confirming previous findings of a distinct 'island' of globally connected parameters.

This article investigates the Dirichlet problem associated with a nonlinear elliptic equation, which involves a critical Sobolev exponent on a bounded domain in R^n and a function. Solutions to this equation, which are periodically related to a known solution of the corresponding limit equation, are examined for their existence, local individuality, and dependence on the domain. A method is proposed to prove n-dimensional periodic solutions, which are then used to demonstrate local individuality and periodicity solutions through careful variations of the domain, a function, and their combined parameter.

Recent advances in code translation models have reached human expert parity on some programming language assessment tests. However, these models frequently synthesize code that appears semantically correct but ultimately fails during execution or produces suboptimal results. Our research indicates that incorporating a basic static analysis layer can effectively identify and rectify such flawed code, enhancing the quality of code generated by state-of-the-art translation models on widely used datasets for the Python language.

On November 4, 2004, a solar neutron explosion was detected at the GOES-12 satellite, with a peak intensity of 2 x 10^-5 cm^-2 cm^-2 s^-1 at 10 MeV, and 2 x 10^-4 cm^-2 cm^-2 s^-1 at 30 MeV, and it lasted for about 10 minutes.  This event was associated with a 2.66 x 10^25 erg/solar second total energy flux from a 1.15 x 10^27 erg/solar second spectrum that resembled a 3.5G 2.66 x 10^25 erg/solar second total energy flux from a 1.15 x 10^27 erg/solar second spectrum that resembled a 3.5G 2.66 x 10^25 erg/solar second total energy flux from a 1.15 x 10^27 erg/solar second spectrum that resembled a 3.5G 2.66 x 10^25 erg/solar second total energy flux from a 1.15 x 10^27 erg/solar second spectrum that resembled a 3.5G 2.66 x 10^25 erg/solar second total energy flux

We have analyzed the dispersion relations for relativistic fluid perturbations that take into account rotation and covariant acceleration acceleration, using the standard first-order hydrodynamics model. Our study is based on the uniform flow assumptions and considers both symmetric and antisymmetric components of the entropy flux. The results in this study build upon previous research but in a more comprehensive way. The dispersion equations in this study, in general, do not describe stable hydrodynamics. The findings in this study, however, are in line with the results of the variational principle applied to the action.

Our proposed anomaly identification framework, InQMAD, utilizes next-generation
quantum processors to detect changes in measured frequencies within intricate
quantum systems. By slightly increasing the complexity of a reference quantum
circuit's structure, InQuiet measures the 'quietness' of measurement outcomes
from a target quantum processor, allowing for effective detection of hidden
anomalies that may be present in high-dimensional spaces. By restricting the
analysis to a specific, low-dimensional quantized frequency distribution,
InQuiet ensures robust performance and minimizes the need for extensive
repeated measurements. By leveraging the inherent efficiency of single-shot
measurements, InQuiet can significantly reduce the computational overhead and
achieve a level of quantifiable sensitivity. By comparing its quantized
frequency data with a reference, it effectively isolates anomalies and
provides a measurable score of 'quietness'. By limiting the analysis to
quantum frequency distributions, it avoids the need to process vast amounts of
raw data, thus ensuring efficient and scalable anomaly detection on high-
performance quantum processors.

The State Coercion Decryption Test (SCDT) is a novel, forced-homomorphic encryption scheme that forces victims to disclose their decryption keys by falsely claiming state authority. We analyze SCDT in the context of forced decryption coercion and discover it fails to protect against such coercion. By examining the underlying mathematics of SCDT, we reveal its vulnerability to artificial calculations that appear to fulfill the state's requirements. Notably, any decryption scheme based on homomorphic encryption can be forced to disclose their keys using SCDT. We also explore the implications of SCDT on the authenticity of cryptographic proofs and introduce a new design, State-Checked Decryption (SCD), which forces victims to confirm their own verification of a cryptographic proof after checking it against the state's requirements.

We present a novel universal framework for analyzing measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution systems. This framework allows any MDI-QKD experiment to be modeled numerically, taking into account the individual and correlated errors in the signaling and measurement components, and automatically calculates the system's secret key rate. Furthermore, our framework is not limited to specific types of error, including binary symmetric errors commonly used in previous studies, but can accurately model more realistic errors, such as Gaussian errors. When applied to an actual experiment, our framework shows a significant improvement in the calculated secret key rate, demonstrating its reliability and accuracy. As such, it provides a valuable tool for designing and evaluating future MDI-QKD systems.

Approximate weighted circuit satisfiability is a key weighted constraint problem that has many applications in other circuit and satisfaction problems. In the classical setting, constant-factor approximation algorithms are limited to very specific types of instances. A new algorithm has been developed that allows for a PTAS in cases where the instance graph has low sparsity, specifically when the number of edges is no more than a fixed multiple of the number of vertices. This algorithm is also applicable to other constraint problems, including list coloring and colorability with pre-assigned vertex weights.

This study proposes a novel numerical technique to solve the advection-diffusion PDE, where the solution is non-negative and may exhibit sharp gradients. The method utilizes a Lagrange-Galerkin time-discretization combined with a non-conforming high-order spatial discretization, utilizing tensor product elements of the DG type. An abstract framework and specific applications to advection-diffusion equations and mean field games are examined. The methods demonstrated retain consistency with the method's key convergence properties.

Within the $U_1$ leptoquark model, two decay processes, $B \to K^{(*)} \mu^+ \mu^-$ and $R_K$ data, can be effectively explained by a single $U_1$ leptoquark through its coupling to quarks and leptons at the first-generation level. However, low-energy $B$-meson decay data suggest that $U_1$ leptoquark is constrained to be quite massive. Consequently, this study investigates the feasibility of describing the $B \to K \tau \bar{\nu}$ decay within the $U_1$ leptoquark leptoquark by considering $U_1$ leptoquark's interaction with first and third-generation quarks and leptons. It is discovered that if the $U_1$ leptoquark does not participate in the $B \to K \tau \bar{\nu}$ decay, it must be extremely massive, but if it is allowed to interact, it can exist as a particle with a moderately low mass of around 3 TeV.

This study examines the level of understanding and explanation of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) using visual representations, as the current DNNs excel at solving complex, high-dimensional pattern recognition problems but lack clear pattern processing explanations. We surveyed 50 undergraduate students to assess their ability to interpret visual outputs from a DNN trained on the MNIST dataset, comparing it to the average human performance. Furthermore, we analyzed the explanation of visual representations by examining the accuracy of explanations that matched the color distribution of the student and non-student DNN visual outputs. We found that (a) the majority of students do not fully grasp the meaning behind DNN visual representations, comparing it to the average human performance; (b) the explanation of the attention maps from the student DNN is better than that of the non-student DNN; and (c) the attention maps from the student DNN provide a better explanation than those from the non-student DNN.

Recent observations have revealed a surprising correlation between the spin rates of young stars and their nearby planets, with particularly fast stars often hosting giant planets very close to them. This discovery has sparked debate over whether the ingestion of small, rocky bodies can slow down stars and facilitate the formation of planetary systems, or if another mechanism is at play in the transfer of angular momentum between stars and their planets. To address this, researchers used observations of the star CD-56 53 to analyze its characteristics and the composition of the material surrounding it, ultimately discovering that even a minimal ingestion of spinning dust could explain the spin rates of this star and the planets around it. This unexpected angular momentum transfer is yet another example of how stars process matter, or that there is another unexplored mechanism for angular momentum transfer between stars and their planets. This discovery also highlights the importance of considering how matter is ingested by stars when analyzing the formation of planetary systems.

Multimodal news posts that integrate text and images are commonly shared on social media, but the prevalence of fabricated news is rising due to their ease of creation and widespread dissemination. Although existing methods for identifying false news are effective, they are limited to specific scenarios where both modalities are available. To address this challenge in single-modal situations, our research develops a flexible framework called Meta Neural Process Networks (MetNPN) that can simultaneously handle single- and multimodal settings. This framework combines emergent multimodality, meaning only both modalities are necessary for some news posts, by drawing from recent advances in neural process networks. By integrating emergent multimodality, our method outperforms current approaches in the multimodal setting and is, to our knowledge, the first to work in single-modal scenarios. Furthermore, our method demonstrates improved performance on a real-world dataset, demonstrating its validity and potential for broader application.
This article examines the periodic transport equation, which models the flow of a substance through a system.

In a discrete time status refreshing system, n independent sources periodically transmit binary data to a central device that processes a binary data unit. The moment when all n sources data units are ready is defined as the period of interest.

This work explores the connection between various mathematical structures, such as associative algebras, monoidal categories, and tensor algebras, and a general class of functions called set-theoretic genre solutions to the Yang-Baxter equation. By introducing quasi-bialgebras as a special type of typed algebra with additional structure, this research provides new, accessible proofs of several important results, most notably showing that set-theoretic genre solutions lead to a weakly equivalent quasi-bialgebra, a result that was previously established in a much more complex mathematical way. It also provides a similar proof for a related result involving ordinary set-theoretic solutions to the Yang-Baxter equation.

A novel class of codes known as complementary multi-phase sequences (CMPS) has been discovered, which may efficiently reduce interference in code-division multiple access (CDMA) systems. Although conventional complementary sets (CS) are effective, their large size in phases or limited number of available sequences are drawbacks. The CMPS codes, however, offer a solution by presenting a two-dimensional array of sequences distinguished by multiple phases and a simple construction technique has been developed, which produces CMPS codes of different sizes and a method of expanding them has also been demonstrated.

In silicon, an unconventional form of quantum entanglement known as valley coherence can be manipulated to create spin currents. This process involves interfering with electrons in different minimum energy points, or valleys, in silicon's electronic structure. An experiment was conducted in which a laser induced a valley current and an atomic point defect was used to transfer that valley information into electron spin. By applying two types of magnetic resonance, both the incoming valley coherence and resulting spin coherence were measured. These measurements allowed for characterization of silicon's unusual two-valley system and provided a method for generating quantum entangled spin states using valley currents.

Complex systems, characterized by their intricate web of connections and interactions between components, frequently exhibit sudden and unpredictable changes in overall behavior.  Understanding such dynamic behavior is essential for providing effective management and intervention strategies.  Despite significant progress in applying graph-based representations and machine learning methods to analyze these complex systems, a holistic approach that integrates their physical, statistical, and dynamic aspects has been lacking.  This document presents a comprehensive graph neural network approach to modeling dynamic relationships and interactions within dynamic, continuous systems represented by their underlying graph structure.  It outlines a set of fundamental graph learning challenges, explores relevant applications in various fields, and proposes an integrated, multi-aspect graph systems understanding framework that leverages graph neural network methods.  This framework is illustrated through a case study of the COVID-19 epidemic's evolution and is further applicable to other systems, such as neuronal networks, financial markets, and epidemic outbreaks.

This study introduces a concept called homotopy divisions within the framework of type theory, extending previous work on explicit division algorithms in the homotopy 2-sphere. By introducing a parameter, a homotopy division is defined as a mapped structure that parametrizes all possible paths between a given element and zero. In the context of algebra, it is shown that R-algebras admit a non-ambiguous homotopy division, which can be applied to construct a homotopy initial algebra.

Certain neurological diseases, such as cerebral lesions, can cause severe damage to a person's cognitive functions and quality of life.  Developing artificial intelligence systems to diagnose and treat these conditions requires a significant amount of data, but obtaining this information from real patients is time-consuming and expensive.  As an alternative, researchers are using computer simulations to generate artificial cerebral lesions, but existing methods often produce unrealistic results that fail to accurately reflect the complexity of real lesions.  In this paper, we propose a novel technique for generating a wide range of cerebral lesions in brain images, based on a progressive adversarial auto-encoder framework.  Our method is based on a step-by-step process, in which latent variables are decoded into images at each stage of the process, resulting in realistic lesions that vary in appearance and complexity.  Experimental evaluation shows that our technique is effective and efficient, outperforming other methods in terms of both image quality and the time it takes to generate lesions.  These results indicate that our approach can provide a valuable tool for training data for diagnosing and treating neurological conditions.

In the field of quantum information, we often utilize nonlocality in entangled quantum states to achieve better outcomes in communication protocols when compared to local states or entangled states that exhibit reduced security. We have discovered that nonlocality in entangled states provides a significant advantage over states that mimic classical behavior in terms of inequality violations, with an average of 2.17 times greater inequality violation. This holds true for frameworks consisting of four to nine dimensions that mimic an unextendible product basis. We have also demonstrated that this inequality violation ratio remains greater than one for all possible combinations of states in HPS. Furthermore, we have verified the nonlocality of entangled states in experimental settings for frameworks from four to eight dimensions, with a violation of the Bell's inequality that is greater than the maximum possible violation by states that exhibit UMP behavior. This finding indicates that non-quantum states in low-dimensional systems can produce a measurable inequality of Bell's nature.

In the latest stage of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, also known as SDSS-V, the Total Secure Coordination of Astrobots (TSCA) will be operating in 2024. This project involves using a group of autonomous robots to manage the positioning of a set of cameras on a rotating platform. Ensuring that these cameras work in unison is essential for their success. A previous study by D. A. Jarque et al. presented before TSCA began, outlined the steps for their operation. A key aspect of their plan is using the total secure coordination algorithm. A previous version of this algorithm was presented at the 2021 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems, where its total secure coordination features were discussed. A more recent implementation of the algorithm was presented at the 2022 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems, where its performance was evaluated under real-world conditions. A setup consisting of astrobots, which are modified Canon cameras, was used for this evaluation. A rotating platform was also used for this test. A key finding was that the secure coordination period of the algorithm is 0.1 seconds. This short period is one of the requirements for the astrobots' operation in TSCA. A key limitation of the algorithm is its reliance on the availability of the necessary computational resources. A key aspect of the algorithm is its ability to handle the variability of these resources. A key feature of

The standard GP 2 compiler is a highly versatile tool suitable for both research and practical applications. Its versatility is due to the compiler's ability to leverage an existing abstract syntax tree, which was originally created for the GRI language. This feature allows GP 2 to rapidly integrate new and experimental language constructs by reusing the abstract syntax tree. However, incorporating object-oriented programming concepts required significant modifications to the parser and symbol table. These changes made it difficult to incorporate such concepts in a library-based approach. In contrast, the new enhanced compiler introduces a new parser that preserves backward compatibility with the GRI language while enabling the inclusion of additional grammars. As a result, a new, intuitive object-oriented programming language called GRI++ has been created and is now available for use in the GRI platform.

UNoCoRe, a unified structure for efficient feature extraction from unstructured data,
leverages comparative unsupervised learning to identify and extract key characteristics.
By organizing data into hierarchical representations that capture relevant attributes,
UNoCoRe facilitates the use of existing machine learning techniques for classification.
The structure's modifiable nature allows for effective handling of concept
changes and data with unknown labels. Notably, when applied to spam detection,
UNoCoRe showcased superior performance over other classifiers even with limited
training data and a significant reduction in processing time.

A novel class of diagrams, referred to as twisted wreath quotient diagrams, is presented here, based on the relationships between subgroups of a specific twisted wreath product. These diagrams are linked to pairs of subgroups within the alternating group of a twisted wreath product, where certain conditions, such as being maximal and self-conjugate, are met by these subgroups. By utilizing methods from research on the symmetry of groups, the authors here demonstrate the existence of up to half of the number of diagrams, with an even number, by excluding one case, and show that these quotient diagrams possess a specific property, described as being 'star normal', under the classification of groups. Additionally, it is proven in this research that the star normal property holds for an infinite number of diagrams, of twisted wreath type.

Working with nominal data in statistical and machine learning models is a significant challenge, particularly when dealing with high-dimensional datasets.
Our research introduces an advanced version of the Group Lasso technique, designed to handle nominal data with high dimensionality.
By integrating a nominal encoding strategy and the Group Lasso method, HLGL effectively handles nominal data without making assumptions about its underlying structure or using alternative encoding techniques that could distort distances.
Evaluations through simulation studies and real-world applications show that HLGL exhibits excellent performance, exhibiting robust stability, strong feature selection capabilities, and competitive accuracy when compared to other learning algorithms.
Introducing a sparsity control parameter into HLGL enables it to achieve optimal fit and accurate hyperparameter estimation, which we demonstrate using the Bayesian Elastic Net framework.

Large, language-based models have recently achieved remarkable success in multiple linguistic tasks thanks to their vast knowledge base. However, there's limited understanding about how prior experience and information within their massive data sets influences their exceptional performance. To address this gap in knowledge, we present a novel framework called ABILITY, which enables the manipulation and integration of specific knowledge sets into these advanced models from huggingface. By combining two primary components, ABILITY first employs a modular module to isolate distinct knowledge domains, and then enhances a secondary module to apply that knowledge to a larger, main model. As a result, we can seamlessly HUG other knowledge sets onto the main model in a completely isolated fashion. Furthermore, this framework can be applied to any type of language task and any specific knowledge set of interest. Through the use of integrated modules, we can precisely locate knowledge in the main model, as well as in additional sets, which can be accessed using a unique language called DQL. To showcase the versatility of our framework, we conducted experiments using HUG modules based on separate memory systems and neural-network-based models. Through these experiments, we were able to demonstrate the ability to integrate distinct knowledge sets into the main model without disrupting existing knowledge, thereby revealing the power and potential of the HUG module.

This study examines a specific type of nonlocal dispersion model, where the rate of change of density at a given location depends on the total travel distances of both pedestrians and vehicles, weighted by an exponential function. The model's limits, both locally and fractionally, are determined and found to be equivalent to each other. The primary method used is the passage to the limit with an infinitely small weighting function parameter, which provides the the the equivalent result with an infinitely large mean weight. Additionally, the model is simplified to this the same form by an alternative approach, involving an infinitely small total travel distances parameter, with a different weighting function. The results are further demonstrated with a basic traffic flow model that transitions to an alternative nonlocal model and a classic local model, either simultaneously or sequentially.

Traditional panoramic stitching techniques are constrained by their reliance on aligned epipolar lines, which can be unreliable in the presence of significant objects in space. A novel approach is proposed, leveraging a statistical prior of gravitational consistency to minimize the computational effort required to stitch images into a panoramic view. This approach is formulated as an optimization problem, subject to constraints reflecting the relative positions of cameras and images in three-dimensional space. By employing a series of carefully selected objective functions, the approach can be reduced to solving a series of quadratic equations, allowing for an efficient solution using standard algorithms. This method is shown to outperform existing techniques in a range of experimental scenarios.

The cancellation of local poles of Eisenstein series is caused by the pole cancellation sums being zero. This in turn is due to the combinatorial properties of the group elements and the application of the Mobius inversion formula, which relies on the discrete mathematics of partial order sets.

Neurodegenerative diseases, including Parkinson's, affect millions of people worldwide and stem from the gradual deterioration and death of specific brain cells. Due to their complex nature, pinpointing the causes and developing effective treatments for these conditions has proven challenging. A significant hurdle in this endeavor is the lack of comprehensive computational models that accurately incorporate biological data and account for the intricate interactions within the affected brain systems. Existing computational models, though useful in various contexts, have primarily been developed for other diseases and often fail to reflect the length scales and complex geometry of the affected neurons. A new approach, called LINC, has been introduced to create integrated computational models by combining finite element models with low-dimensional neuron models. This study demonstrates the potential of this approach by developing a comprehensive, data-driven biophysical model of the Parkinson's disease in marmoset primates. Utilizing the LINC approach, this model simulates the release of dopamine from the substantia nigra and its subsequent uptake in the striatum, ultimately facilitating reward-based behavior. As various parameters in the model are altered to mimic the effects of neurodegeneration, characteristic symptoms of Parkinson's disease, such as bradykinesia and akinesia, are observed. Furthermore, this comprehensive model can be used to test potential therapeutic interventions and guide the design of clinical trials.

When line layers are combined, a single pixel may contain up to six different line junctions. To accurately depict the geometry of GML and SVG maps, an anti-aliasing technique has been devised. By utilizing a line width lookup table (LLUT) and pre-rendering line junctions into 2x2 and 3x3 pixel blocks, a method has been developed to eliminate color fringing effects. This technique was implemented in the Mapbox GL engine and can efficiently render line junctions with a color frame.

We conducted 9 deep 6-metre class observations with the Seimei telescope and the KOOLS-IFU, targeting gas kinematics and chemical composition in 51 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies. These targets have a redshift less than 0.04 and exhibit extreme merger activity. By analyzing spectral line intensity maps of [O III] $\lambda$ 5007, [N II] $\lambda$ 6549, H$\beta$, and H$\alpha$, the KOOLS-IFU data enabled us to derive ionized gas velocity fields and abundance maps. Notably, we observed highly elongated N-Kyr gas structures in several galaxies. These gas formations are likely created by the gravitational interaction and possible jet activity from central supermassive black holes. Gas with abnormal chemical composition are also observed in a couple of galaxies. Such anomalies could be a result of gas mixing from tidal tail mergers and gas transport due to central jet activity. Additionally, we observed significant gas anomalies in the central regions of some galaxies. Such gas anomalies could be a result of gas mixing from tidal tail mergers as well as gas transport due to jet activity. In summary, the KOOLS-Ifu data allows us to investigate gas anomalies and their formation mechanisms in detail, providing crucial insights for understanding galaxy mergers.

The multivariate interpolation problem is addressed by traditional methods, 
however, they struggle with extensive data sets and exhibit the phenomenon of 
oscillation increase with variable polynomial degree. This paper presents a novel 
transcendental radial basis function, which is then utilized to develop an 
interpolation operator that maintains form and exhibits quasi-optimal convergence 
properties. The proposed operator exhibits an $O(h^2)$ error rate in the $\infty$-norm 
and an $O(h^2)$ error rate in the $L^2$-norm, which can be elevated to an $O(\min\{2,s\})$ 
$L^2$-norm error rate when the function being interpolated possesses higher smoothness. 
The proofs of these results are supported by rigorous mathematical analysis.

Accurate weather categorization is crucial for the safety and efficiency of various systems, including aviation, urban planning, and disaster prevention.  While several techniques exist for analyzing precipitation using radar images, the results can be inconclusive due to the complexity of the task and the influence of multiple factors on weather patterns.  As a consequence, current methods for weather classification often yield unsatisfactory results.  In response to this challenge, we have created a novel dataset consisting of 150,000 radar images spanning 10 distinct weather categories, encompassing both day and night scenes.  To address the issue of data imbalance within this dataset, we have developed a data augmentation strategy tailored specifically for radar images.  Our experiments, conducted using this dataset and various classification algorithms, have revealed the importance of addressing the issues of data imbalance and widget scaling in achieving accurate multi-class weather classification.  Our approach employs Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for this purpose, and the most effective algorithm achieved a macro F1 score of 0.8595, corresponding to a 15% improvement over the baseline using our data augmentation strategy.  Moreover, we have observed that existing weather classification methods tend to favor certain categories due to the influence of training data, and that addressing this bias is essential for successful implementation.  Our work provides a foundation for future research on this challenging task and highlights the critical role of data quality and balance in achieving accurate weather classification.

To restore the original speech quality, a single talker can be restored from a recording containing multiple talkers by modeling the dual path of convolution and recurrent networks. This novel approach, called the Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network, combines an attention mechanism for enhanced representation learning and uses a multi-channel input to learn features related to speaker identity and location from the unseparated speech. Experimental results show that the proposed network's dual path design leads to speech quality improvements, with the attention mechanism also resulting in better performance when evaluated using the multi-channel dataset.

A combination of modified gravity theories and particle physics can significantly influence the size of dark matter halo clusters at their boundaries. Specifically, modifying general relativity through an $R^2$ gravity model and considering neutrinos with masses of $0.06$ eV to $0.12$ eV can alter the radius of these clusters. By integrating the gravitational model and neutrino masses, researchers can determine the turn-around radius of cluster dark matter halos and compare it to an $\Lambda$CDM model model. This study indicates that an $R^2$ gravity model would require lighter neutrino masses to produce the same turn-around radius as gravitational forces would be amplified, allowing halos to expand to a larger size. Conversely, heavier neutrino masses can counterbalance forces, restricting the halo's expansion. This study also indicates that the $g$-factor in the $f(R)$ gravity model should not exceed $10^{-3}$ to remain consistent with cosmological observations.

This study aims to develop a multi-fluid model for simulating Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection, with a view to linking it to atmospheric convection. By adapting the formulation from atmospheric convection models and using the assumption of non-reacting fluid mixing, we implemented a two-fluid simulation with differing gas properties and non-ideal gas laws. At high Rayleigh numbers, bubble formation and collapse patterns mirror those observed in single-fluid simulations but with notable differences in the size of convective features. Specifically, the model produces smaller boundary layers and smaller bubbles due to the influence of gas properties on the flow dynamics. When the heavier fluid experiences greater resistance to heat transfer, it sinks in distinct plumes, with the overall convection pattern dictated by the characteristics of the non-rotating system.

This research examines how quantum entanglement develops among multiple independent particles that interact with separate cavities under the Jaynes-Cummings model.  We investigate the point at which particles become entangled and analyze the entanglement's growth over time, especially in a set up with three particles.  Our findings show that the type of initial particle states impacts the onset of entanglement, and in a three-particle system, there are distinct periods of collective and individual entanglement.  Moreover, our analysis reveals that there are entanglement phases where all particles are involved, and others where entanglement is limited to pairs, offering useful insights for designing entangled states of multiple particles using Jaynes-Cummings interactions.

The CMS Pixel Detector is an essential component of the LHC's muon detection system, contributing to the precision tracking of particle trajectories at the interaction point and edge regions of the detector. It enables the formation of jets from hadrons and helps in reconstructing energy deposits from photons and muons. At the interaction point, advanced tracking capabilities are achieved with upgraded readout chips, enabling the retrieval of up to 600 million sensor hits per second. However, in other regions, the rate of single muons from heavy-ion collisions is not fully covered by the original chip, limiting their functionality. As such, the upgraded central detector chips are replaced, but at the edge regions, they are supplemented with additional chips that capture a extra layer of information. This results in a mismatch in detection between the two sets of chips and hampers the reconstruction of particle trajectories. This project aims to develop a method for combining data from both sets of chips in the pilot edge regions of the Phase-1 CMS Pixel Detector, specifically during heavy-ion collisions. By analyzing the performance of this reconstruction method in simulated and actual data from the ALICE experiment at the LHC, the outcome shows that it can match the precision of the central detector while providing a more balanced increase in tracking performance across all regions of the upgraded CMS Pixel Detector.

Using a Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral depiction approach, we have successfully
  identified the ground state mass and excitation masses and moments for the lightest
  scalar glueball in SU(2) QCD. Through exponential scaling and Leutwyler-Stern
  sum rules, the necessary input data for this analysis is obtained from lattice
  simulations. The masses are derived from the oscillatory pattern in the Euclidean
  Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral depiction, while the excitation data is extracted via
  spectral fit procedures. The analysis yields a mass for the lightest scalar glueball
  of 2.38(9)(6) GeV.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis is crucial for tracking the public's emotions. Recent studies have focused on developing effective sentiment analysis techniques using Natural Language Processing and Machine Learning, with a particular emphasis on Long Short-Term Memory networks. Despite numerous combinations of preprocessing methods and auxiliary systems being tested, there is a need for a more transparent and reproducible evaluation process. To address this, an open Sentiment Evaluation Framework is proposed, consisting of four distinct components: data preprocessing, feature extraction, classification, and performance assessment. This framework has been validated on four benchmark datasets, documenting specific details about each step to facilitate the creation of additional evaluation modules.

A novel framework, referred to as modified corresponding state law (MCSL), has been developed to analyze the thermodynamic properties of charged black holes in anti-de Sitter (AdS) space through the lens of the holographic thermal density operator (HTDO) within the context of the gauge/gravity duality. This approach contrasts with traditional methods using the grand canonical potential (TCP). By applying the HTDO framework and incorporating the effect of the photon mass, researchers discovered that the thermodynamic behavior of non-linear charged black holes follows a pattern where the reduced chemical potential correlates with the square root of the dimensionless horizon temperature. Specifically, this relationship indicates that the horizon temperature of a non-linear charged black hole is directly proportional to that of a linear charged black hole when their respective parameters are identical. Furthermore, analysis of the heat capacity and entropy revealed that as the photon mass increases, both quantities decrease for a linear charged black hole in both small and large regimes, whereas the opposite effect is observed for a non-linear charged black hole in the large regime.

A new method is proposed to quantify changes in a tomogram's entanglement state and identify the point at which two systems' entanglement patterns start to align. This approach is demonstrated using the Werner state as input, and the entanglement measure employed is the negativity.

Developing conversational agents that can engage in meaningful discussions with people is a complex task due to the vast amount of knowledge they need to process. Current methods, which are based on narrow领域的 models, often require significant computational resources to connect the model to the agent. One alternative approach is to use smaller, specialized models that are already capable of exchanging information with users. However, this approach is limited to the specific domain in which the model is trained. In this paper, we introduce a novel strategy for defining the role of a conversational system and then utilize a large-scale language model to build a system that can engage in meaningful discussions across a wide range of topics. Our approach is based on a single, unified loss function that optimizes the language model to produce the desired output. We also present a new, openly accessible dataset containing more than 50,000 conversation pairs centered around the topic of music. Experimental results show that our method effectively achieves the defined role of the conversational system while also engaging users in natural and enjoyable discussions.

The problem of pest control in strawberry plant recognition is a complex, real-world issue. To effectively manage strawberry pests and diseases, it is crucial to develop accurate detection and classification methods. In the food industry, the safety and quality of products are increasingly dependent on pest control. While various approaches have been proposed for strawberry disease classification, a vast number of pesticide options complicate the process. This paper presents a novel, robust method for identifying and classifying pests and diseases in strawberry plants, utilizing a data set of 16000 labeled images. By training and evaluating a series of deep learning models, including CNN, Inception V3, ResNet-50, and MobileNetV2, a specific architecture demonstrated the highest accuracy of 99.93% in Strawberry disease classification.

360-degree video technology is being used in tourist videos to create immersive experiences that allow viewers to feel like they are physically present at the destination. However, due to 360-degree videos being recorded from a single point in space, travelers must manually navigate and rotate the camera to explore their surroundings. The primary challenge lies in the lack of realistic interactions in the 360-degree videos, which results in an unrealistic experience for users. As research into the factors that influence individuals' attention and visual perception continues, a new model called CapVNet has been developed to predict future viewports in 360-degree travel videos. CapVNet takes into account not only contextual information from the destination and surrounding objects but also the underlying mechanisms of human visual perception to inform viewport predictions. Furthermore, a new dataset called AVID, which contains a vast array of diverse scenes, has been created to evaluate the effectiveness of viewports prediction models. Research has shown that incorporating human perception into prediction algorithms improves the accuracy of future viewports significantly.

Tensor network techniques are widely utilized in studying complex quantum systems, 
yet they struggle with representing thermally equilibrium states due to maximal 
entropy even when the reduced density matrices of subsystems are in ground states. 
To address this issue, we modify the tensor structure to incorporate "blobs," 
which can accurately represent thermal states while maintaining linear or quadratic 
scaling with the number of sites. By doing so, a single layer of these modified 
tensor networks is sufficient to approximate thermal states in a way that is 
efficient and precise for a specific temperature threshold. When the temperature 
is above this threshold, a single layer is sufficient, 
but two layers are required for lower temperatures. The temperature dependence 
of the precision of these models is investigated, and it is discovered that 
they converge to the correct thermal state in a power-law manner. The cutting 
edge research indicates that a specific type of modified tensor structure called 
the "twisted imaginary time algebraic tensor network" represents thermal states 
most effectively. To further explore the limitations of this approach, we 
demonstrate that it is impossible for a single polynomial-sized region to 
approximate a thermal state without violating physical constraints. The 
efficiency of these algorithms is demonstrated by successfully applying them to 
thermal states in various models, including the transverse-field Ising model, 
the Hubbard model, and the Schr\"odinger-Hagen model. The results are summarized 
in a comprehensive table.

This research explores decoupling effects in limited success scenarios and
multi-organism scenarios involving shared resources. We analyze these situations
by creating simplified models that incorporate randomness and apply these models
to restricted success and resource competition cases. Firstly, we examine a
1D structure consisting of alternating good and bad sites, where particles are
placed on the bad sites. These particles attempt to move to the good sites with
a probability p and stay in place with a probability 1-p. It is shown that a
significant number of particles can survive, even when p is less than one.
Moreover, it is demonstrated that, in scenarios involving a large number of
particles, only the positions of a small number of particles significantly
affect the distribution. This result is analogous to the concept of decoupling.
Moreover, the model can be solved exactly in situations involving randomness
that depends solely on the site's characteristics.
Moreover, we examine a model in which p is less than one and p is greater
than one based on p.
Alternatively, it is shown that the exact results can be achieved using a
model in which p is always less than one. This result is analogous to a
restricted form of route decoupling.
Moreover, we derive an equation for restricted efficiency in terms of random
numbers that depend solely on p. This provides a basis for the simulation of
restricted efficiency in scenarios involving a large number of organisms.

In this research, we develop a nonisotropic version of the relative Minkowski inequality concerning capacity. This inequality provides a bound for the nonisotropic relative $p$-capacity with respect to sum of mappings, and implies an inequality similar to the relative Minkowski inequality for convex bodies. Additionally, we derive the inequality similar to the Minkowski's inequality for the points of minimal nonisotropic capacity.

The MICROSCOPE space mission, which took place between 2016 and 2018, involved two ultra-sensitive accelerometers with significantly reduced technical noise. These accelerometers tracked the test of the weak equivalence principle at a high level of precision in a controlled, uniform environment. As part of data analysis, a comprehensive methodology was developed to identify and assess the impact of outliers on the experimental results. This methodology was applied to the complete dataset collected during the mission, which consisted of nearly 330 days of measurements made in a uniform environmental condition. Our analysis revealed that, when accounting for anomalies, the deviation from unity in normalized acceleration differences does not surpass the 95% confidence level of 1.64 standard deviations and remains within the 95% confidence level of 0.64μG plus 0.10μG, which combines statistical and systematic uncertainties.

We investigate the behavior of non-interacting particles that are subject to an activity gradient. This gradient causes a variation in the particle activity level, resulting in an effective force field. In regions where the activity is symmetric, this effective force has a repulsive effect, which is responsible for pushing the more mobile particles away from areas of low activity. The distribution of the more mobile particles is found to be described by a power law with an exponential correction, in contrast to the distribution of particles with decreasing mobility, which follows a compact pattern.

A minimum strong shortest path cover of size k-1 in a graph G with k vertices is equivalent to its k-Strong Shortest Route Cover problem. This paper investigates the k-SSRC for graphs that have a limited number of vertices, including those with a maximum of three vertices per cycle, those with a maximum of five vertices per cycle, and general network structures. Additionally, we explore the k-SSRC's applicability in solving the water supply network design problem.

The presence of renormalons in the color dipole gluon distribution's small-x behavior has been investigated, and a non-zero contribution from two-loop renormalons was found, in contrast to the Gaussian contribution which vanishes due to color algebra, and a impact parameter dependence which may aid in distinguishing it experimentally.

To analyze the frog model's behavior on a specific type of random structure, we examine how many frogs will eventually become inactive, or 'die out', based on whether they visit already-checked branches. We prove that, under the condition of finiteness, the number of doomed frogs grows exponentially with the size of the tree, but if there are infinitely many frogs, there will be some that do not become doomed with certainty. Additionally, we determine the final state of the tree when there are infinitely frogs, which is finite but unpredictable based on the number of frogs. This result has further implications for understanding the extinction of species in certain ecological models.

Two-dimensional metallic arrays exhibit strong light-matter interactions with incident photons due to their near-field lattice resonances, and this effect can be optimized by separating the conduction electrons from the ions using a dielectric substrate. This research investigates the relationship between the dielectric substrate's permittivity and the two-dimensional photonic lattice's resonance, specifically for a hexagonal gallium phosphide substrate and aluminum indium gallium phosphide array. Findings show that increasing the metallic layer's thickness shifts the resonance frequency, and for thinner metals in the MIM regime, the resonance is influenced by the gallium phosphide substrate's high-Q factor, resulting in an anisotropic resonance map. However, in the PMC regime with a thicker metallic layer, the resonance returns to being symmetric, demonstrating that two-dimensional metallic arrays on dielectric substrates can be used for resonance sensors that respond to orientation changes and in-switching devices.

This research explores zero-shot knowledge transfer from a decision-based
black-box framework, specifically a torsion balance, which accelerates learning
by utilizing a decision framework in contrast to binary yes/no queries like those
used in the master app learning task. Thanks to this transferability, we can
achieve similar master app knowledge with just a single device, regardless of its
specifics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the enhanced efficiency of the
torsion balance can benefit other tasks beyond the initial learning and transfer
applications, specifically by enabling the creation of more sophisticated
concept models in the 2D shape domain.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L$ decay mode for the first time, with a significance of 4.2 standard deviations, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L$ decay mode. By combining results from two analyses, they have determined the branching fraction for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L$ as $3.70\pm0.11(\textrm{stat})\pm0.04(\textrm{syst})\times10^{-4}$, and the lower limit for the branching fraction of $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L$ as $0.62\pm0.10(\textrm{stat})\pm0.05(\textrm{syst})\times10^{-4}$, assuming similar values for the decay modes of $K^0_L$ and $\bar{K}^0_L$.

We present an efficient method for constructing the lattice of submodules of a specific type of module, known as multiplicity-free, over a group ring. This specific approach leverages the lattice of submodules of a direct sum of group rings, which serve as critical components of the module in question. The method enables a faster construction of the lattice for submodules of a specific type of module, which relies on the lattice of submodules of a direct sum of group rings. This method is then applied to determine the lattice of submodules of a particular module, which serves as a specific example of the method.

A strong geodetic set for a given graph is one where every edge in the graph can be found on at least one shortest path between two designated vertices within the set. Determining whether a graph contains a strong geodetic set of a specific cardinality is a known NP-complete problem, for which a geodetic parameterization algorithm is available. In a recent study, our objective was to examine a more restrictive variant of this problem, known as the strong geodetic identification problem. This variant seeks the minimum cardinality of a strong geodetic identifier set for a given class of graphs. Unfortunately, a surprising result emerged - almost all classes of graphs for which the strong geodetic identification number can be efficiently computed also exhibit the same property for the general strong geodetic set problem. This implies that solving the strong geodetic set problem may be computationally difficult using a specific algorithm, or that finding strong geodetic sets of a certain cardinality might be impossible. A specific example was provided - the strong geodetic set problem is impossible to solve for cubic 3-connected bipartite graphs with at most an exponential number of bits representing the input. This result also indicates that the strong geodetic identifier number for such graphs is at least $\frac{n}{3}$ and that the same problem is cardinality-based NP-complete for planar bipartite graphs. Additionally, the strong geodetic identification number is at most $\frac{2n}{5}$

The task of mimicry learning focuses on training agents to replicate optimal behavior from observed demonstrations. A key challenge in this area is efficiently utilizing available data, which includes both optimal demonstrations and observations from a shared environment. While several methods exist for mimicery learning, they often struggle to effectively utilize subpar data, resulting in performance that is significantly worse than the demonstrated behavior when access to the environment is limited. To address this issue, we propose a new algorithm called TRAIL, which leverages a theory-based regulation approach to enhance the use of subpar data. Our results show that TRAIL outperforms existing state-of-the-art algorithms by a considerable margin, achieving up to a 10x improvement in efficiency and matching or surpassing demonstrated performance in several tasks without near-optimal data. Furthermore, TRAIL exhibits robust generalization capabilities, outperforming competing algorithms in terms of generalization accuracy.

Reinforcement learning has been effectively applied to complex, real-world tasks through collaboration between agents and human instructors who guide the agents using reinforcement signals. However, having agents learn solely from displayed expert knowledge necessitates meticulously preparing and training complete expert models. An alternative approach is observing and evaluating both expert and non-expert agents, which is feasible with just access to the expert model and the ability to interact with the learning subject. This method is more practical for working with standard systems that cannot be easily modified but requires further development to prevent the learning agent from being content with suboptimal solutions. We suggest a framework for co-observation reinforcement learning, allowing for the extraction of multiple types of signals from the observation process and suggesting the use of separate display learning and self-estimation display comparison methods. We tested this approach in two experiments: a simple task and a cart-pole swing-up task, and found that co-Observation Reinforcement Learning enabled successful improvement of performance when combined with display learning and self-estimation display comparison learning.

Personalized Attention Control has long been recognized as a beneficial feature in broadcast television and has recently been explored in the context of partial attention scheduling for cognitive radio networks. This paper proposes an entirely new approach to measuring user focus in television broadcasting, employing machine learning technology to assess user attention levels and automatically adjust the personalized control settings. By utilizing this approach, broadcasters can fine-tune content based on real-time attention levels and prevent viewers from becoming bored or losing interest.

Previous studies have shown that applying reinforcement learning (RL) after supervised learning can improve translation outputs, particularly in scenarios with limited action spaces. This work builds on this by investigating RL in the context of fully extensive action spaces in TNMT. Initially, a simple RL approach is implemented to learn the optimal supernet among a network ensemble generated through supervised learning. The RL framework is then expanded to allow the RL agent to learn individual network structures and edge supernet weights in TNAS. Experimental results using ResNet on the MNIST dataset demonstrate the superiority of our proposed methods over traditional TNMT techniques.

Achieving precise 3D position estimation of a robot's end-effector using a depth camera is crucial for effective robot manipulation.  However, due to the complex nature of robot kinematics and the statistical limitations of depth cameras, raw depth data is often inaccurate.  As a result, the calibration of the camera and adjustment of the kinematic model are necessary.  Unlike previous approaches, we propose a novel, unsupervised learning approach to simultaneously learn the optimal camera settings and end-effector position from robot manipulation videos.  Unlike manual calibration, our approach doesn't require labeled images or a complex optimization process.  Instead, it automatically learns from unmarked robot manipulation videos.  Unlike typical camera calibration, our approach can accommodate any arbitrary camera configuration and is capable of learning the optimal camera settings using only straightforward loss functions, regardless of the robot's kinematic model.  Unlike typical end-effector position estimation, our method allows for manipulation videos without marked objects and achieves precise 3D position estimation through unsupervised learning.  Unlike typical reinforcement learning approaches, our method doesn't require a complex reward function or policy optimization process.  Instead, it directly learns from robot manipulation videos that the robot attempts to grasp and push an object to a 3D position.  Unlike typical multi-view geometry approaches, our approach doesn't require a complex scene reconstruction or multi-view optimization process.
